title: When a Nation's Supports Collapse
overview: Isaiah warns that Jerusalem and Judah will lose everything they rely on, because their leaders crush the poor and the people openly defy the LORD.

parts.label: Every support taken away (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The LORD will remove everything Judah leaned on: food and water, soldiers, judges, prophets, elders, skilled workers, even the fortune tellers people trusted. Many readers link this to the Babylonian conquest, when leaders and craftsmen were carried off into exile.

parts.label: Chaos without real leaders (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Immature rulers take charge, and society turns on itself: neighbor against neighbor, young against old, nobodies against the respected. Anyone who still owns a decent coat is begged to lead, and he refuses because he has nothing to repair the ruins with.

parts.label: Open defiance and its harvest (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Judah is falling because its people defy the LORD openly, flaunting their wrongs like Sodom, a city remembered for shameless evil. The good are promised good and the wicked harm, each reaping what they did.

parts.label: Bad leaders on trial (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Verse 12 says the people are ruled by "youths" and "women." This may mean the rulers are weak and unfit, or that women at court held real influence; an ancient Greek translation reads "creditors" instead, so scholars are unsure. Then the LORD takes the elders and officials to court for ruining his "vineyard," an image for his people, and for filling their houses with what they took from the poor.

parts.label: Proud women stripped of finery (vv. 16-24)
parts.note: The wealthy women of Jerusalem, parading their status, will lose every item listed here, from ankle bells to mirrors, and face disease, ropes, sackcloth and branding instead, harsh images of being marched off as captives. The Hebrew of verse 17 is unclear and may mean baldness from disease or being publicly stripped, a common humiliation of captives.

parts.label: A city in mourning (vv. 25-26)
parts.note: The men will die in battle, and the city is pictured as a woman sitting on the ground in grief. Even the city gates, once the busy heart of public life, are said to mourn.

think: When a society's leaders fail, how much of the blame belongs to them and how much to everyone else?
